script: In 1996, scientists cloned a sheep from a single cell - and named her after Dolly Parton for a very specific reason. July 5th, 1996, the Roslin Institute in Scotland. Researchers took the nucleus from an adult sheep's mammary gland cell and fused it into another sheep's egg cell. It took two hundred seventy-seven attempts. Dolly was the only lamb who survived. The name came from a lab assistant's joke on the spot - since the donor cell came from a mammary gland, why not name her after Dolly Parton? Dolly became a global celebrity, and sparked a real fear: if you can clone a sheep, could you clone a person? In 1999, researchers found her cells had shortened telomeres, and a theory spread that clones age faster than normal animals. In 2003, Dolly was put down at six, with lung disease and arthritis. Scientists said it probably wasn't from being a clone - other sheep in her flock got sick too. Dolly Parton, when she found out, said she was flattered. Follow for more true stories with a twist nobody expects.

metadata.title: Random But True: Why The First Cloned Animal Was Named Dolly
metadata.caption:
July 5, 1996, the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh, Scotland. Researchers fused the nucleus of an adult sheep's mammary-gland cell into another sheep's egg cell - the first mammal ever cloned from an adult cell.

It took 277 attempts. Dolly was the only lamb born alive.

The name was a lab assistant's on-the-spot joke: since the donor cell came from a mammary gland, why not name her after Dolly Parton? Dolly Parton later said she was flattered when she found out.

Dolly became a global celebrity and sparked real debate: if you can clone a sheep, could you clone a person?

In 1999, researchers found her cells had unusually short telomeres, fueling a theory that clones age faster. In 2003, Dolly was euthanized at age 6 with lung disease and arthritis - but Roslin scientists said this likely wasn't connected to cloning at all. Other, non-cloned sheep in her same indoor flock got the same lung disease, and later cloned sheep (including genetic copies of Dolly) have aged completely normally.
